anya: Heads-up — telemetry spike: we're seeing a small but consistent set of cache hits attributed to tenant A that actually served responses for tenant B. Not a full data leak, but cross-tenant cache key reuse. Putting the sample stats below.
kevin: ugh. numbers?
anya: From 03:40–04:10 UTC: 0.028% of prefix cache hits flagged as 'cross-tenant' by our collision detector (pipeline: cache-telemetry -> dedupe-fingerprint). 85% correlate with kernel v3.2.1 canary.
ops-bot: deploy-bot: canary rollout of runtime/kernel:v3.2.1 started at 1976543000.
sangeeta: do we know the key derivation? I thought we included tenant_id in the HMAC.
anya: current derivation (simplified):
```
cache_key = trunc256(sha256(salt || model_hash || prompt_fingerprint))
```
We used global salt per-region to enable fast warmup reuse across tenants. That was an explicit design choice to improve hit-rate for similar prompts.
maria: oh — global salt sounds risky for isolation. But it probably helped hit-rate. Any evidence collisions are from truncation?
anya: yes. The collision set has identical first-160 bits of sha256. When we truncated to 128 bits for index, that amplified collisions.
derek: maybe kernel scheduling changed request ordering so different tenant requests ended up in same batch more often and hit same kv shard? Could explain the v3.2.1 correlation.
kevin: good call. v3.2.1 changed batching heuristics (adaptive-window) and sharding affinity for KV reads to reduce tail latency. That could change co-location patterns.
sangeeta: tradeoffs: global salt + truncation improved cross-tenant warmup hit-rate by ~2.1%, saving tokens, but now introduces collision surface. Need a mitigation plan that balances perf and safety.
maria: quick ideas: 1) include tenant_id in HMAC input (cheap), 2) stop truncation to 256-bit store key (storage perf hit), 3) per-tenant salt (harder for warmup sharing), 4) per-entry envelope encryption with tenant KMS.
anya: I prototyped hmac(tenant_id || model_hash || prompt_fingerprint) — compute adds ~0.9us/op on hotpath in microbench. Batching masks it mostly but kernel-level scheduling may matter.
derek: ops concern: per-tenant salt breaks cross-tenant warm hits which will regress latency/cost for multi-tenant RLHF workloads that reuse prompts. Could we do salt-rotation + prefix namespace: keep global salt for warmup-only keys but mark them non-sensitive and avoid returning payloads from those keys unless tenant matches?
sangeeta: that adds complexity and risk of returning stale/wrong data if we mis-mark. Also increases audit surface.
kevin: short-term: revert kernel v3.2.1 canary on regions with highest collision rate and roll a patch to include tenant_id in key derivation (HMAC) + remove truncation to 160 bits. That should eliminate reuse collisions without full per-tenant salt.
maria: can we measure perf impact? Run A/B: current vs HMAC-tenant + 160->256 bit. Need microbench and canary litmus.
anya: I ran a local microbench: HMAC+full-256 increased median KV lookup time by +0.8us, p99 +1.6us. For typical 4-token gen paths that's within SLO but will increase cost a bit.
kevin: ok schedule: 1) pause v3.2.1 canary in EU (ops-bot already flagged), 2) roll hmac-tenant patch to canary channel, 3) run 24h litmus comparing hit-rate/regressions, 4) pick permanent strategy (per-tenant salt only if still problematic).
derek: we should also add an audit hook that records anonymized collision vectors and which kernel/batch they were in so we can correlate in future.
sangeeta: also add a small nightly job to scan for truncated-key collisions and alert when rate > 0.01% for 1h.
maria: agree. let's add ticket and owner. tagging infra and security. :+1:
kevin: I'll open the rollback + patch PRs. Anya, can you attach a minimal reproducer (trace + cache key dump) to the PR?
anya: will do. attaching sanitized logs. Note: removed tenant content body, left fingerprints and key prefixes.
ops-bot: incident-bot: scheduled rollback for runtime/kernel:v3.2.1 in eu-west-1 at 1976543500.
maria: thanks all. followups in #eng-security and I'll coordinate KMS/crypto review.
kevin: thx — keep updates short here.
